subject: cerberusPup
pitch:
Category: Fantastical creature.
Subject: three-headed puppy.
Style: your choice. Pick an unexpected, striking visual style that suits this subject (not the obvious one), name it in a comment at the top of the module, and commit to it everywhere.
reasoning:
I'm thinking through an unconventional visual style for depicting Cerberus—weighing options like a Victorian clockwork toy versus a hand-stitched felt plush with embroidered details, trying to pick something unexpected rather than the obvious choice.

Alebrije feels like the winner: a Mexican folk-art style with vividly painted carved wood, dots, swirls, and flowers, which suits a fantastical three-headed creature perfectly. I'm sketching the puppy's proportions—chunky body, three heads with distinct color schemes, separate jaw joints, floppy ears, a curled tail—and planning to layer on alebrije-style patterns in hot pink, turquoise, yellow, orange, and other bold colors with dotted and striped details, now working out the overall scale at roughly 0.55 meters long.

Working out the leg and spine skeleton with joint positions...

Actually I'll place hips at [0,0.30,-0.12] and build the spine chain from there instead, keeping naming simple even though it's not perfectly anatomical. For the body sweep I'm considering extending the end radius with a flat cap versus a rounded one.

Working through the body sweep for the chubby puppy torso, running from z=-0.13 to 0.17 with round caps that add extra length at both ends, giving a rump around -0.25 and chest near 0.30, for a total body length of about 0.55. I'm tuning the radius function so it bulges slightly in the middle while staying thick enough at the chest and rump ends.

Now I'm designing a festive alebrije-style paint for the body, combining a base color with diagonal stripes and dot patterns using cell-based noise to scatter dots and a gradient coordinate to create the stripe bands.

Writing paint function logic...

Thinking about texel density for the paint resolution — at 2048 the dots should read clearly at roughly 1mm-1cm scale, so that'll work. Now I'm sketching the three-headed structure: necks branching from the spine's last joint, with the center neck going up and forward and the two side necks angling outward, each terminating in an oversized puppy head.

I'm working out joint naming and parenting for the neck chains — deciding whether the head should be the chain's tip joint or a separate joint parented to the neck's last segment so it can carry its own "head" role, with positions and angles fanned out so the three heads don't overlap.

For orientation, I realize using local "forward/up/left" words works cleanly for the center head, but gets tricky for the outward-angled side heads since their yaw means model axes no longer line up with each head's own facing direction — so I'm sketching a small helper that applies forward/up/left offsets relative to each head's own rotated frame instead of the global axes.

I'll define a helper that mirrors a point across the frame's own axes so left/right features reuse the same local coordinates, then move on to placing decals like eyes using head-relative direction vectors.

As an alternative to decals, I'm weighing textured sphere eyes, but that approach has the drawback of needing a distorted double-width texture to compensate for spherical UV wrapping, which feels clunky.

Instead, I'm thinking large round alebrije-style eyes with concentric rings and eyelashes would fit better, placed as a plane or circle geometry conforming to the curved skull surface via a decal technique for a more seamless look.

I'll build an eye texture factory that generates several iris/ring variations, then construct each head with a function that assembles the skull sphere and scaled features per spec.

For the muzzle and jaw, I'm using frustum-box shapes attached to the head joint for the upper jaw, with the lower jaw as a separate part on its own joint, sizing dimensions per head variant with the center head slightly larger.

Still working out head coordinates...

Working out the lower jaw geometry now: positioning the jaw bone and its frustum box in pink tones, adding a small red tongue slab and tiny white fang cones, and calculating the z-offsets so the muzzle and jaw surfaces meet cleanly for a closed mouth.

Since the jaw is built as a separate bone, I can give the center head's jaw a slight downward tilt around 12 degrees, giving it a cute panting, tongue-out look for that puppy.

Now I'm extruding a rounded tongue shape attached at the jaw bone, keeping it flat and horizontal with thickness running vertically, positioned near the front top of the jaw so it moves naturally with the tilt.

I'll color it pink and let it extend slightly past the muzzle front with a downward tilt for a lolling effect, reserving that only for the center head's open mouth -- side heads instead get a smaller tongue poking out sideways.

I'll give each head distinct personality: left head does a small blep with closed mouth, right head stays closed with a tiny smile and a fang poking out. For the ears, I'm placing floppy extruded shapes rooted at the skull's top-side, defining their outline in a local (outward, up) plane with a painted alebrije-style pattern.

Working out the ear orientation vectors now, mirroring left/right sides and curving the outline downward so the ears hang naturally, with thickness running along the forward axis so they stay flat and visible from the front.

Adjusting the tilt direction so the ear axis makes the outline hang down and splay slightly outward at the bottom, which matches natural floppy ear shape better.

Shaping the ear outline...

Naming the ear joints uniquely per head (left/center/right) while keeping valid identifier syntax, then moving on to placing eye decals on the skull surface at the appropriate position and size.

For positioning I'm using the surface-query approach: calculating azimuth and elevation angles from the skull center to place each eye symmetrically, relying on the hit normal to orient the decal direction outward correctly.

Now I'm adding little eyebrow bumps slightly above each eye using the same angular offset trick, then considering whether to add glow effects anywhere—deciding the eyes themselves won't glow but perhaps collar gems or tail flames could.

I'm leaning toward giving the tail a flame-tufted tip in alebrije style, rendered as a glowing SVG card texture on a crossed plane, since the card-based glow approach works well with the mesh system. The nose stays simple—dark with a highlight, no glow needed there.

For body decorations, I'm placing marigold flower decals (SVG petal rings in orange/yellow with a bright center) as surface decals on the hips and back, sized around 0.1. For the collars, I'm sweeping a ring around the neck using a surface loop cut at the neck's midpoint, adding diamond studs along the band.

I'm also thinking through attaching beads along that neck loop by sampling points along the path and placing small spheres at each one, making sure the bone inheritance from the frame carries through correctly since items placed on a point inherit that point's bones. For the legs, I'm planning a simple chain-based IK setup — front legs with shoulder and paw targets, segment lengths, and bend directions (elbows bending back, knees bending forward) to keep the puppy's stance chunky and simple.

The legs convert into a polyline path, parented to the appropriate spine or hip joints. For skin, I'm varying the sweep radius so the thigh is thicker than the lower leg, adding a haunch bulge for the hindquarters, and building chunky rounded paws with small toe marks, a dark pad, and tiny claw cones—making sure the paw bottom aligns with the ground plane.

Then I'm applying sock-colored gradient paint near the bottom of each leg and stripe patterns for the alebrije look. For the tail, I'm defining a curling chain of three joints rising upward from the hips, parented to the hip joint, and sweeping it with a tapering radius.

Adding a glow flame at the tail's tip, making sure the tail root starts inside the body near the rump rather than floating outside it. Overall the puppy's silhouette comes to about 0.65 in height, with the tail curve and flame fitting comfortably within that range.

Now I'm working out the neck and head placement: the neck should originate inside the chest cavity and curve forward and up to meet the head joint, with the skull and muzzle positioned so the head's total forward reach stays proportional to the body length.

For the side necks, I'm angling them outward with a slight yaw so the left and right heads splay away from center, but I need to check that the ears on adjacent heads don't overlap or collide given how close the skull centers end up.

For the center head's ears, I should scale them down to avoid collision with the side heads—the inner ears of the side heads sit close to x=0.175, so the center head's outer ears need to flop outward slightly to clear that gap.

Now I'm sketching the neck as a tapering sweep with chain-like striped segments connecting to the skull, then thinking about adding fur tufts and feather-like dorsal ridge decorations in true alebrije style.

For the spine, I'm planning to place a series of small painted cones along the body sweep, alternating colors with a counter since the path callback doesn't guarantee an index. Then I'll add dotted whisker details on the cheeks and small fang cones in the jaw.

For the fangs, I'm figuring out cone orientation so the tips point downward near the muzzle corners, aiming for well over 200 parts total once multiplied across all heads. Now I'm sketching out the texture list, starting with multiple eye variants showing iris color rings against a white sclera with dark outlines.

I settle on eight textures total: three eye variants, marigold flower, spiral swirl, flame, cheek tuft, and a chest sun medallion, skipping the collar pattern in favor of painted sweeps. I start laying out the SVG structure for the eye texture with alpha-transparent edges.

Writing SVG code...

Building the spiral path with looped point calculations for the swirl, then moving to a flame design using a red-orange-yellow gradient for a glowing effect.

I'm sketching a simple tuft shape and a sun medallion with triangular rays in gold for the chest motif. Settling on an alebrije color palette—vivid pink, teal, yellow, orange, purple, blue, green, cream, ink, and red—and planning the head colors as warm orange-yellow against a turquoise body with pink and yellow accent motifs.

Working out distinct hues per head (hot pink with yellow, purple-blue with teal, orange with green) while keeping the body a consistent turquoise-blue with pink bands and yellow dots, and matching legs/paws to purple-yellow bands and orange tones. Writing the paint function...

I'm confirming negative k values work fine with the bitwise parity check in JS. For the sphere heads, banding across z creates vertical ring sheets front-to-back across the face — a bit decorative but acceptable.

For the skull, I'll parameterize banding with a direction vector and frequency rather than a fixed axis, so heads can get swirl-like diagonal bands while eyes decals still render on top without being obscured. Now I'm double-checking API specifics: confirming createBuilder accepts a paintSize option, then moving on to review the joints setup.

Setting up the hip joint and spine chain, then sweeping a tube body along the spine with a radius function controlling thickness at each point for a rounded, tapered torso shape.

Continuing the chest curve up to the neck area, with the tail base set lower on the spine, and I'm working out how to place flower decals on the body by raycasting against the flank surface to find hit points for attaching them.

Setting up the neck chain sprouting from the chest spine joint, then defining a head joint attached at the end of the neck chain with the right direction and role tagging.

For the head's orientation, I'm working out the dir vector for side heads pointing slightly forward and up, normalized so the aim calculation behaves correctly, then using local-space axes to position the head frame while keeping roll consistent so the creature's right side stays oriented properly.

Now I'm sketching the skull geometry itself — a scaled sphere attached to the head bone, where the scale needs to align with the head's local frame so the ellipsoid stretches along the head's forward axis rather than world axes.

I'm defining a small helper function that creates a head-attached part positioned via `head.local()` and oriented using `head.axis`, so other features like eyes or ears can reuse it while still letting individual calls override the direction when needed (e.g. cones pointing elsewhere).

Now I'm working out the muzzle geometry using a frustum box between two points on the head, aiming it with a default roll so the width runs along the binormal axis and height along the normal -- keeping a blocky puppet style rather than smoothing it, though I'm considering adding a nose sphere and cheek bumps for character. I'm also starting to set up the jaw joint, positioning it relative to the head using local coordinates.

Adding the whisker dots as small decorative spheres in rows on the muzzle, then planning fluffy cheek tufts using card elements scattered across the sides of the skull.

I'm considering alebrije-style head accessories — maybe tiny horn nubs or spikes on each head, and a decorative crest fin running from forehead to back on the center head, outlined as a zigzag polygon in a contrasting color band.

I'm also deciding how to vary the three heads: a crest fin on the center head, curly spiral horns on the left head, and something distinct like a pompom or antenna shape on the right head to keep each one visually different.

Writing curved horn geometry...

Thinking about the right head's decoration now — maybe a small flower crown made from a ring of petal spikes arranged around a point on the head, using a ring helper to place each petal outward.

Writing spike parameters...

I'm figuring out where to anchor the medallion on the front of the collar, finding the nearest surface point facing forward, then placing a decal there with a sun texture so it reads as a glowing medallion print rather than a separate geometric piece.

I want to make it emissive so it looks like gold catching light, wrapping the decal with a glow effect, but I need to be cautious since glow has specific material requirements and any mismatch could throw an error. I'll also use the same decal approach to scatter marigold flowers across the body surface.

For top-facing flowers I need to override the default up vector to avoid degenerate orientation when the sample direction is straight up, while flank flowers can use the default. I'm also planning dorsal spines along the back using a sweep-based placement helper, positioning cones at intervals along the body's spine.

For the tail, I'm using a glowing upward card at the chain's tip, oriented by the frame facing along the tail's tangent, to create a flame effect at the very end.

Now I'm rigging the tail tip to its bone for proper deformation and adding a small gold bead at its end, then moving on to the paws: for each leg, I'm placing a scaled sphere as the paw, bound to the wrist bone, with plans to paint it orange with ink pad accents on top.

For the toe details, I'm placing three small cream spheres near the front of each paw and skipping visible claws since they'd be hidden, verifying the geometry stays above ground level so nothing clips below zero.

Now I'm shaping the haunches with chubby thigh blobs at the hips and smaller shoulder blobs up front, then adding cuff rings around the legs using a loop along the bone sweep near the shin.

Checking that the cuff loop placement is safe since it sits on the centerline where the surface definitely intersects, even through smoothed blend zones. Now I'm turning to the body surface for scattering decorative elements like flowers and a cream chest ruff, filtering by position and normal direction to target the chest area.

I need to check that cells, noise, rgb are exported from the main SDK index, and that kits like glow come from their own subpath import. For the open mouth, I'll rotate the jaw by 14 degrees, making sure I build all the jaw geometry first before applying that pose transform.

Checking the rotation math: a positive 14° rotation about the X-axis correctly tips a forward-pointing bone downward, confirming the jaw will open as intended. For the eyes, I'm working out the skull center position and scaled radii, then using surface raycasting from that center at specific azimuth and elevation angles—with azimuth 0 pointing forward and 90 pointing right in the model's local frame, adjusted for the head's yaw.

I'm setting eye azimuth as a function of yaw plus a fixed offset so the eyes sit naturally on either side as the head turns, with elevation around 12° and decal size scaled to about 6.5cm to look appropriately cute on a 17cm head. For brows, I'm positioning them higher at elevation 38° and using a flattened, stretched sphere stick oriented along the surface normal, with a slight spin rotation to angle them expressively based on side.

Now I'm placing the nose as a small ellipsoid sphere at the muzzle tip, colored ink with a sheen, positioned just above the muzzle's upper edge. I'm defining the muzzle as a cream-colored patch with dots as an accent rather than pure alebrije coloring, and starting to lay out the head specification object with neck points, direction, scale, yaw, and color assignments for the base, accent, band, dot, muzzle, and iris.

I'm filling out the eal/ring color, mouth opening angle, tongue size, and crest fin for the middle head, then specifying mirrored left and right side heads with their own neck points, directions, scales, yaws, and distinct color palettes including horns, tongue blep, and flower details — with the right head mirroring the left by negating x. I'm also working out naming conventions for the neck joint chains and confirming the parent chain attaches to the last spine joint.

Now I'm reasoning through how the three necks converge near the chest, overlapping slightly at their base radius before spreading, and how each neck sweep should taper into the skull with a rounded cap, using the head's color palette for painting. I'm also starting to tally up the total part count across body, legs, cuffs, paws, haunches, spines, and flowers to estimate the model's complexity.

Then I'm counting all the per-head components (skull, muzzle, teeth, ears, eyes, horns, etc.) across three heads to reach roughly 230 total parts, well within budget, and deciding which elements should glow -- the flame and medallions, but not the nose or tongue.

Starting to write the import statements for the build script...

Still defining palette and helper functions...

Adding lighting and color mixing...

Now I'm estimating performance: with up to ~3M painted texels at 2048 resolution, each running a 27-cell noise lookup plus hashing, I'm guessing roughly a few microseconds per texel, putting total compute somewhere around 5-10 seconds — acceptable but worth keeping an eye on.

At default 1024 resolution the model's painted surface area (~1.5 m²) gives texels around 1.5mm, which is plenty of density for 6mm dots (about 4 texels across), so 1024 should be sufficient while 2048 would just give crisper dotted lines. I'll lean toward 1024 as the default for speed.

Now I'm sketching out the SVG texture generator for the marigold flower, building concentric rings of petals with ellipse shapes whose size, radius, and color shift per ring.

Now I'm building a spiral path for the hips, computing points along an expanding radius as the angle sweeps around to create a swirling line shape.

For the outline I'm applying a two-layer stroke, ink underneath and color on top, then adjusting dot sizing proportionally to fit the 192px target. I'm sketching a flame shape using a curved outer path that tapers at the top and bottom with a filled gradient.

Now I'm defining the flame's color gradient going from golden yellow at the top through orange to a reddish-crimson at the bottom, plus a smaller inner cream-yellow flame layer for depth. I'm also sketching a leaf-shaped tuft icon with a center gray stroke line, and planning a sun medallion with twelve gold ray triangles around a central circle with an inner dot ring.

Now I'm shifting to the actual character build function, setting up the builder and a seeded random generator, then constructing the skeleton starting with the hips as root joint and a spine chain built from a catmull-rom curve through several waypoints with named sub-joints.

For the body mesh, I'm sweeping along the spine with a tapering radius profile and painted texture, considering whether to use faceted (flat-shaded) geometry instead of smooth circles since this is meant to evoke a wood-carved alebrije aesthetic.

I'll apply flat shading consistently across body, legs, necks, and tail for that carved look, then move on to building the leg structures using the limb helper, bending each pair outward and working through how the bend-direction argument should be shaped for a two-segment limb.

Now I'm figuring out reach distances for the front legs and setting up the chain that connects shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints to the spine, then sweeping a tapered profile along that chain to form the leg geometry. Moving on to set up the hind legs next.

Still working out leg joint positions...

Since tip may be null but hind legs have enough names, I'll use a non-null assertion on leg.tip there. I'm placing paw ellipsoids slightly above ground and offset forward from each foot position.

Now I'm setting up the cuff rings by taking a loop cross-section partway along the leg sweep and sweeping a thin yellow hexagonal tube around it, inheriting the skin weights from that point. I'll skip adding dots on the cuff.

For the tail, I'm building a chain of three joints along a curved path and sweeping a tapering tube around it with rounded caps, then adding a small gold sphere bead at the tip bone. Next I'm starting on dorsal spines running along the body.

I'm placing a row of small cone spikes along the back using an alternating color palette, stopping short of where the neck begins so they don't overlap. Then I'm positioning flower decals on the flanks and hips using ray-projected placement with mirrored left/right coordinates and slight z-offsets to follow the body's curvature near the rump.

I'm also writing a helper function that raycasts against the body surface to find a hit point and normal, then applies a decal there if the ray connects -- guarding against the undefined `up` parameter breaking default orientation when destructured, and noting that the surface query re-reads the mesh after posing so it stays accurate.

Then I'm scattering fur tuft points across the chest region (filtering by height and surface normal so tufts only appear on the forward-facing upper body), generating leaning, bent cream-colored card geometry from those scatter points to represent fur texture.

Now I'm starting the buildHead function, which takes a head spec (id, scale, yaw, palette) and constructs a neck chain from a catmull-rom spline, parented to the third spine joint with named neck joints and a "neck" role tag.

I'm defining the head joint attached to the end of the neck, then sweeping a tapering radius profile along the neck for its mesh shape, and setting up helper functions for positioning head parts relative to the head bone's local coordinate space, using a loose typing approach for the optional part parameters to avoid strict type conflicts.

Now I'm building the skull as a scaled, faceted sphere positioned slightly forward and up, and the upper muzzle as a tapering frustum box running forward from the skull toward a narrower front end.

Still writing muzzle paint and nose geometry...

Now I'm setting up the jaw joint and defining its frustum shape, connecting it to the head at an aim point for the mouth opening.

For coloring, I'm using a flat accent color for the jaw mesh, then considering teeth detail: upper fang cones anchored to the head bone and small lower teeth on the jaw bone, deciding to skip a chin tuft for simplicity.

Still positioning fang cones...

For open-mouth poses, lower teeth would only show when the jaw is open, so I should only add those tiny teeth for the mid/open head pose. Similarly, the lolling tongue should only appear on the mid and left poses.

Writing tongue geometry...

For the middle dog, I'll make the tongue longer with a droop since the jaw opens wider, while the left blep dog keeps a shorter tongue. Now I'm thinking through the ear joints and extrusions.

Setting up ear roots and hinge joints...

The ear's normal is roughly along x, so it reads as a thin edge from the front and flat from the side. Floppy ears should splay outward about 30° with the plane tilted partly forward, and the outline's top needs to attach at the root on the skull side.

I'm computing the root position relative to the skull sphere, checking that the ear emerges from inside the skull by about 1.3 cm so the attachment reads naturally, then laying out the ear outline coordinates relative to that root point.

With the outer outline done, I'm scaling a smaller version around a point lower on the ear for the inner-ear detail, then assigning colors from the palette for the outer and inner ear surfaces.

Now I'm working on placing the eyes by sampling points around the skull mesh symmetrically on both sides, then decaling the eye texture at the hit location oriented along the surface normal.

Checking overlap near the muzzle edge, I bump the eye azimuth up to 52 degrees to pull the eyes clear of the muzzle boundary, then recompute the resulting x/y position against the muzzle's half-width there.

Working through the geometry, the eye position lands near x=.067, forward=.11, up=.044 at this angle, which puts it right around where the muzzle box extends to, so I'm checking whether the eye would actually be visible or occluded there.

I try increasing elevation to 28° and then 30° at a 48° azimuth, recalculating x=.0554, forward=.108, up=.07, trying to get the eye spans clear above the muzzle's top edge so it isn't buried inside the muzzle geometry.

Thinking about brow placement now—maybe around elevation 52-55° at azimuth 42°, though that risks conflicting with the eye position, so I'm considering skipping brows entirely or using small alebrije-style dots above the eyes instead.

For head orientation, I'm working out the azimuth-yaw relationship: the side multiplier times 48 degrees plus the yaw offset, where positive yaw means leaning left. Checking this against the actual head direction vectors confirms roughly 15-16 degrees for each side.

I'm also thinking about a small forehead decoration—maybe reusing the marigold flower decal at a reduced size, centered on the forehead with appropriate orientation matching the skull's curvature there.

For cheek tufts, I'm setting up a scatter of small cards on the skull mesh filtered by normal direction to target the side-lower areas, with tuft size, lean, and bend parameters tinted toward a cream color to distinguish them from the base fur.

Now I'm working out whisker dot placement — three small ink-colored spheres per side positioned on the muzzle's top surface, computing the muzzle's center z-offset and half-height at that cross-section to find the correct radius and placement coordinates.

For the heads, I'm differentiating their features: the middle head gets a crest fin extrusion, a big tongue, and an open jaw; the left head gets horn sweeps and a small blep tongue; the right head gets a flower on top, a closed mouth, and a fang, with sleepy eyes for a shy expression. I'm now sketching out the crest fin extrusion logic for the middle head, figuring out how to orient it using the head's axis and direction vectors.

Still working out the crest's base position relative to the skull and sketching its outline coordinates...

I'm setting an origin point just inside the skull so the crest only pokes out where it exceeds the skull's top surface, then sketching zigzag spike shapes rising above that baseline to form the crest outline.

I check the point sequence for self-intersections and confirm it closes cleanly without crossing itself, then plan to scale by S and color it with a gradient function that shifts from orange at the base to yellow near the tips, plus some thickness and bevel values for the extrusion.

For the horns, I set up the extrusion directions along the head's forward and up vectors, then sketch a curved spline of points sweeping outward and upward from the base to form each horn's shape, using a tapering radius so it starts thick and ends pointed, with alternating pink and cream color bands along its length.

I'm checking placement so the horn base stays tucked inside the skull surface near the correct coordinates, then I realize the ears would overlap with the horn roots, so I reposition the ears lower and more outward and verify the eye location sits in front of the horn base to avoid collisions. I also start placing the flower feature on the second head, centering it just above the top of the skull.

Writing ring spike code...

Assigning distinct extras per head (mid crest with open mouth, horns with blep, flower), then I'm building gold collars with pink beads looping around each neck, plus a front medallion, using a surface loop anchored at the neck midpoint.

I'm sweeping that loop into a hexagonal collar band, then placing beads slightly above the band along a second lifted loop so they sit distinctly on top rather than inside the collar.

Now I'm positioning a medallion on the front of the neck using an angular offset tied to the neck's yaw, but I need to check whether the head's muzzle and jaw geometry would end up overlapping or hiding it at that height.

Lowering the collar and medallion placement to sit beneath the chin keeps the silhouette clean, so I'll settle on a joint position around t=0.3 along the neck path.

Now I'm sketching out the type definition for head palette fields -- base, band, accent, dot, ring, muzzle, jaw, collar, bead, iris, iris ring, cheek, horn -- before moving on to body decoration patterns like alebrije-style bands running across the torso.

I'm also planning the belly countershading (a wavy cream patch where the normal faces downward), separate sock and paw coloring for the legs, and now defining the full color palette object...

Now I'm assigning colors across the body and heads: teal base with purple bands for the body, yellow-based legs with blue bands and pink paws, and pink/purple/yellow tones for the mid head to keep the whole creature riotously alebrije-colored.

For the left and right heads, I'm pairing violet with teal and lime accents on one side, and orange with blue and green accents on the other, giving each head its own distinct but harmonious palette with contrasting muzzles and jaws. I'm also settling on bright teal and yellow tones for the iris details to make the eyes pop.

Writing eye texture SVG...

Actually I realize the lashes would extend past the viewBox boundary, so I need to shrink the main eye circle radius down to around 40 to leave room for lash strokes at the corners.

I'm checking the svg size param, then planning the decal textures needed: eye marks, marigold, swirl, sun, flame, tuft—eight total—and figuring out where marigold and swirl decals go on the body plus their colors.

Sun gets gold with orange, and I'm deciding the tail flame glow should use the FLAME texture rather than marigold. Writing the card setup for the flame glow attached to the tail joint...

For the glowing medallions I'm checking that the decal's returned Part object correctly falls through to the mesh property check in the glow function, since it lacks an isMesh flag—confirming that path works fine. Now I'm turning attention to the hind paws and leg details.

Setting up the imports and type definitions for the alebrije paint system, including RGB tuples, vector helpers, and the options type for base colors, bands, dots, rings, and wave parameters...

Still writing paint logic...

Checking the dot scaling for the stipple cells—working out cell size relative to body size so radius comes out around 5mm, which seems right for typical density.

Building out the full creature structure now—hips joint, spine chain, and body paint with teal base and purple banding.

Defining leg and paw palettes...

Adding paw geometry details...

Now building the hind leg chain with hip, knee, hock, and ankle joints, checking that the segment lengths sum enough to reach the target distance comfortably.

I'm now adding a haunch sphere attached to the hips bone for shape, then starting cuff rings as decorative sweeps along each leg's path.

Finishing the cuff ring sweep, confirming the loop placement and radius give a protruding ring. Next I'm planning the tail, head loop specs, and then body details like flowers, tufts, and spines before finally returning the root. I'm also noting that ear geometry and other extrusions use a typed outline with smoothing set to 1, which should work fine since there are no sharp corners.

I need to watch for a potential error where a tight corner cut crosses another edge when smoothing is applied — this could be risky for the crest's sharp spikes, so I'll set smoothing to 0 for the crest and keep moderate smoothing for the ear outline since its corners are spaced enough to avoid crossing. The bevel on the crest should be small, and I'm adding a helper function to properly type the outline points as coordinate pairs scaled by a factor.

Now I'm defining the head specification type with properties for id, side, neck points, direction, scale, yaw, palette, textures, and animation values like openness and tongue position, then writing the buildHead function that constructs the neck chain from catmull-rom points, attaches the head joint at the end of the neck, sweeps the neck geometry with a tapered profile and colored material, and begins setting up the skull paint and collar details.

I'm working out the skull paint parameters using the palette colors with wave distortion, confirming the skull sphere's low-poly segmentation, and placing a forehead decal based on an angular lookup on the skull surface — then checking whether that decal would be visually obscured by the crest geometry running along the top of the head, since the crest spans nearly the full length and width there.

For the forehead decal placement on each head type, I'm computing its position relative to the muzzle and eyes to avoid overlap, adjusting the decal size down slightly to clear the eye sockets, and settling on a consistent elevation angle across all head variants while verifying the mid-head crest doesn't visually intersect with it given the crest's forward extent and base height.

Still computing crest height curve...

Scaling the spike coordinates by S, then moving on to the mouth, eyes, and brow placements, computing the brow height position using the skull curvature and yaw offset.

I'm checking for overlap between the brow decal and the eye region since their z-ranges intersect, so I'm bumping the brow's elevation higher to avoid the eye's top edge being covered.

Now I'm working through type checks for the joint and tip properties before moving on to writing the medallion decal placement code on the neck using the wrap-around positioning helper.

I'm checking whether the collar band's thickness and lift would physically intersect the medallion decal, and adjusting their heights slightly so the collar sits above the medallion rather than overlapping it.
